units.en: Additionally, divisions have increased breakthrough (⟦0⟧⟦1⟧) but reduced attack (⟦2⟧⟦3⟧) while being protected by their transports. These effects fade away⟦4⟧ as the landing progresses and the troops leave their landing crafts, measured by movement progress (usually ending after 48 hours⟦5⟧). The ⟦6⟧ modifier gives units a head start in this landing progress and reaching normal combat effectiveness sooner.
The ⟦0⟧ modifier primarily provided by later landing craft technologies has two separate effects:
it is additive with the ⟦0⟧ starting breakthrough bonus, but fades away as well;
it multiplicatively improves the landing penalty: the effective penalty is (⟦0⟧ + ⟦1⟧) multiplied by ⟦2⟧(0, 1 − ⟦3⟧ ÷ 3.5).⟦4⟧

Unless invading divisions have captured a port or a city, they might be cut off from ⟦0⟧, and need to achieve these objectives within 72 hours before supplies run out. A floating harbor will provide a temporary supply hub in the landing province, giving the invaders a few weeks to secure an alternative supply source.

A paradrop is a battle plan order that uses ⟦0⟧ to land one or more paradrop-capable ⟦1⟧ onto a target ⟦2⟧. The paradrop order button is available in the battle plan toolbar for an army with at least one paradrop-capable division. After selecting the button, the player must left-click the province of an ⟦3⟧ that contains a minimum of 50 transport planes and then right-click a province that is within transport range as the paradrop destination.

Executing a paradrop order requires sufficient transport planes for the number of divisions assigned to the order (by default, 45 planes per division) and either neutral or 70% ⟦0⟧ in all required regions.

In order to be paradrop-capable, a division must contain only paradrop-capable battalions among its line battalions and support companies. Paradrop-capable divisions will have a checkmark on the parachute icon at the top left of the ⟦0⟧ window. Paradrop-capable battalions are indicated by a parachute symbol in their unit icons during battalion selection. Currently, only the ⟦1⟧ battalion is paradrop-capable as a line battalion. Paradrop-capable ⟦2⟧ are listed below; all other support companies are not paradrop-capable.

Creating a paradrop order requires a minimum of 50 transport planes available at the originating air base.⟦0⟧ Air bases that have this minimum will be highlighted blue during paradrop order creation. To be considered available, transports must not be assigned to other ⟦1⟧, must not be in transit, and must have sufficient fuel supply via the local ⟦2⟧.
After order creation, executing a paradrop order requires 45 transport planes available per division⟦0⟧ assigned to the order at the departure air base. This requirement may be modified as follows:

If the general commanding the divisions has the ⟦0⟧ commander trait, he will have access to the ⟦1⟧ ability, which decreases the transport plane requirement by 10% (i.e., base requirement * 0.9) for seven days at the expense of 0.1 ⟦2⟧ per battalion.
With the DLC ⟦0⟧, the special forces doctrine Strategic Air Lift Corps reduces the transport plane requirement by 50% (i.e., base requirement * 0.5).

If both Glider Planes and Strategic Air Lift Corps are active, their benefits stack multiplicatively (i.e., base requirement * 0.9 * 0.5). Neither modifier overrides the 50 plane minimum for a given paradrop order, but they effectively discount the planes required for two divisions and up.
The table at right provides a summary of transport plane requirements for up to 12 divisions given any active modifiers.

If launching multiple orders from the same air base, the same transport planes will be used multiple times for different orders in waves if there are enough planes for individual orders but not enough for all orders to go simultaneously. Upon selecting the execute button, these orders will launch in waves automatically in the sequence that they were created and will continue to the last order unless the requirements for later paradrop orders are no longer met (e.g., insufficient air superiority in the required regions or insufficient planes for remaining orders due to aircraft losses). Each order takes about 4 to 8 hours to complete, so the biggest disadvantage of executing in waves with fewer planes is the extended time of the overall paradrop effort, which may give the enemy time to react.

The transport wings assigned to a paradrop order must be adequately supplied in order to take off. When transport wings lack the fuel to fly, they will be treated as unavailable upon executing the paradrop order. Reducing supply consumption in the province of the air base or improving supply infrastructure should resolve this issue.

Each paradrop order is targeted on one destination province, whether in friendly or enemy territory. Paradrop orders targeting friendly (own or allied) territory may be executed at any time. Paradrop orders on non-allied territory require a state of war to execute.

The destination province must be in range of the transport wing, which may vary depending on the technology level of the planes within the wing. In-range provinces are indicated with green highlighting during order creation after selecting the departure air base. Provinces belonging to an air region whose geographic center is outside of the transport wing's range will not be considered in range, even if the individual province is within the range ring of the transport wing.

There must be either neutral air or a minimum of 70% air superiority in the departure, enroute, and destination regions of paradrop orders in order to execute.⟦0⟧ Neutral air is defined as the absence of any friendly or enemy air missions in the air region.

If multiple paradrop orders pass through different air regions, those that have sufficient air superiority in their applicable regions will launch, while those that do not have air superiority will not launch. It is possible to have momentary air superiority in some waves but lose it in later waves. When air superiority is regained in the required regions, the pending waves will automatically launch.

The paradrop mechanic provides several interface components that provide information about paradrop orders. Some of the information in this interface is non-intuitive, so the below guidance is provided.

Execute Button – The green execute button above the army icon displays a tooltip on mouse hover with information that is common to all army orders. For paradrop orders, this tooltip will also indicate if insufficient air superiority in one or more affected regions will prevent order execution. Unlike naval invasions, there is no progress bar or countdown number as paradrop orders do not have an arbitrary preparation time and can launch as soon as assigned paratroopers are at the field along with transport planes.

Paradrop Order Arrows – Paradrop orders appear on the map between the departure air base and the destination province. Text on the arrows display the name of the order, number of divisions, and transport planes assigned to the order. If no divisions are assigned to an order, it will appear ghosted. Prior to executing the order, the arrow will be solid and static. Upon executing, the arrow will become dashed and animated until the transport planes actually start launching, at which point it will be dashed and static. This may give the impression that the order is not working, but paratroopers should start landing in their drop-zones within a few hours.

Paradrop Order Arrow Tooltip - Hovering over a paradrop arrow will display a tooltip with more detailed order information, as well as alerts if there are insufficient transport wings or the presence of division ⟦0⟧. The tooltip will not display if hovering over a body of water, only over land.

The insufficient transport wings alert displays before and during order execution if there are not enough transport planes available at the air base for any reason (number of planes, planes on other missions, insufficient supply, etc.). The additional required transports is indicated in terms of wing numbers, rather than individual planes, so it tends to be a vague indicator. The insufficient transport wings alert may also display in the tooltip during order execution even if there are sufficient transports and paratroopers are dropping.

The division attrition alert indicates that the division is losing strength and will perform poorly if launched. Division attrition alone will not prevent launching the order, but presence of attrition may indicate poor supply in the area, which may prevent the transport planes from launching due to insufficient fuel.

Once a paradrop executes, the division may suffer losses if its paradrop is disrupted. These losses will be between ⟦0⟧⟦1⟧ to ⟦2⟧⟦3⟧ of the division's strength, including ⟦4⟧⟦5⟧ to ⟦6⟧⟦7⟧ of its ⟦8⟧ and ⟦9⟧⟦10⟧ to ⟦11⟧⟦12⟧ of its equipment, with an additional potential ⟦13⟧ amount of randomness to all factors regardless of the actual amount of disruption. These losses can occur even when the target province is empty, i.e., when it does not have an enemy division in it. Based on repeated tests of the same drop (i.e., the same order form the same save file), such losses do not seem to be dependent on ⟦14⟧ (i.e., it happens even when at 100% air superiority), but ⟦15⟧ can contribute to how much a division is disrupted.⟦16⟧ Such losses also seem to occur much more frequently when the drop is at higher latitudes (e.g., in Norway or Northern China), or into coastal provinces.

Divisions are paradropped at ⟦0⟧ of their organization, regardless of whether they were disrupted or not. They receive a ⟦1⟧ penalty to their recovery rate for 120⟦2⟧ hours afterward. They also receive a ⟦3⟧ penalty to their attack and defense in combat for 48⟦4⟧ hours.

To make paradrops more effective, a player can use the ⟦0⟧ ability with a commander who has the ⟦1⟧ trait. This allows paradropping divisions within the next 7 days to land with a lot more organization (up to ⟦2⟧) and take fewer losses from disruption, though this comes at the cost of ⟦3⟧.

A Front Line is the starting point of attacks into enemy territory. A player can either assign a whole country's border as a front line by clicking on the border or a player can assign a part of a country's border as a front line by holding the right mouse button and dragging the mouse over the provinces the player wants to belong to the front line deployment area. The AI will then move all the divisions into the position that the commander assigns to that front line. They are assigned either by having them selected when the front line button is clicked or added later by selecting them and Control-Clicking on that line. A player can also create several unconnected front lines and assign divisions between them, which may be particularly useful for a ⟦0⟧ who may command an unlimited amount of ⟦1⟧ conducting various operations in different locations around the world. Divisions that are stationed at a front line that borders a non-ally will receive a planning bonus for their pre-attack preparation time. Front lines can only be positioned at a border, and the front line of battle between opposing forces counts as a border for this purpose.

An Offensive Line is a line that a player draws through enemy provinces that contain objectives for the assigned army units to move to and capture. From a front line, or from another offensive line, a player can draw one or several offensive lines or arrows that tell the AI how the player wants the selected plan's divisions to advance from the front line. The width and arc of the offensive line can be adjusted as described on the tooltip. If the mouse cursor is dragged over the offensive line or arrow the game will show the exact visualisation of how the AI will advance the divisions, step for step. ALT for edit mode and TAB to shift the arrow's base can be useful to direct the main effort.

The order to execute battle plans is given with the button above the commander portrait, along with a tooltip that provides information and advice from the staff regarding the battle plan. The AI then executes the battle plan until the troops reach their offensive line which has then become the new front line. If that front line has offensive line orders beyond it then the execute button has to be pressed again to resume the advance from the new front line. Pausing to rest, resupply, refit, regroup, and coordinate further plans was common between phases of a major offensive. This is also a good time to detach troops to consolidate control over occupied territory, which usually involves smaller divisions that specialize in discouraging unrest. The Garrison Area battle plan order is one used in such a situation.
More examples for front line and offensive line

The spearhead order starts from a front line and can be used alongside or instead of the Offensive Line within an army. Unlike the normal battle plan that spreads out to cover its flanks and adjusts to circumstances, spearheads advance in a narrow path one province wide to their objective, exactly as it was when first defined. This makes them suitable for blitzkrieg-style armored penetrations that can capture a specific goal or work with another spearhead pincer to encircle enemy cities or armies in pockets, sealed in a ring of steel by the mobile and regular infantry divisions following behind. Encircled armies can thus be annihilated, as routed divisions which lack friendly territory to retreat to are destroyed.
